sections.html:
• Name: Red Fin Dwarf Pleco
  • Other names: Red Fin Otocinclus, Red-Tailed Otocinclus, Red Oto, Minute armored catfish
  • Scientific name: Parotocinclus maculicauda
  • Water type: freshwater
  • Minimum tank size: 15 gallons (~60 litres)
  • Keeping: medium
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Size: 1.6–2.4 inches (4–6 cm)
  • Temperature: 68–79°F (20–26°C)
  • pH: 5.5–7.5
  • GH: 1–10
  • Dwellers: bottom to mid-dwelling
  • Nitrate: less than 40
  • Diet: detritivorous
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Life span: up to 5 years
  • Colour: light brown with small black spots
This species is not very hardy and requires careful attention to water quality and temperature to thrive and breed. It is therefore not recommended for beginners.

This species is mostly found in the south of Brazil (southeastern coastal rivers of Brazil, from Santa Catarina to Espirito Santo). There are also some reports that Parotocinclus maculicauda has been observed in different coastal rivers of the Atlantic Forest.
These fish typically inhabit the bottom of slow and fast-moving rivers, often near rocks and logs, in association with submerged vegetation, where they graze on the biofilm.

The minimum recommended tank size for a group of 5–6 fish is 15 gallons (60 litres). Despite their small size, they should not be kept in small tanks due to their active behaviour. Additionally, they need horizontal swimming space more than depth.

Poor water quality can greatly affect their lifespan. Key stressors include temperature, pH, oxygen levels, ammonia, nitrite and nitrates. Cycle your tank before bringing fish home, then check the water quality with a test kit.

Substrate

In the wild, they thrive among mud, rocks and boulders, so it is best to replicate these features. Avoid coarse gravel, as its sharp edges can harm the fish. On a sand substrate they may even burrow a bit, with the tail sticking out and the head buried. Large stones provide a lot of surface area for biofilm and other microorganisms to grow.

Decorations and plants

They require plenty of hiding places, such as caves, driftwood, twigs, tall plants, leaves, pipes and floating plants. They may retreat there if threatened or stressed. Some aquarists believe driftwood is essential because the fish nibble on it, which helps digestion; what is certain is that driftwood quickly develops a biofilm they enjoy.

Plants

This species can be kept in planted tanks. Generally they will not eat healthy plants, but while feeding they might accidentally harm plants with soft leaves.

Temperature: 68–79°F (20–26°C). They can tolerate fluctuations up to 86°F (30°C) quite easily, as practical experience has shown, and can be a good choice for cold tanks.

pH: 5.5–7.5. In the wild they thrive in slightly acidic water.

Hardness: soft to medium water is preferable; anything in the 1–10 GH range is acceptable. They do not like very hard water.

Nitrate: less than 40.

Lighting: Subdued lighting is best. In planted tanks, lighting should be adapted to the needs of the plants.

Flow: In nature they inhabit shallow streams and rivers with slow or even fast current, and they like to swim in it. They can be kept without a current without being significantly affected.

Aeration: A powerful filtration system is needed to aerate the water and maintain high oxygenation, as the fish enjoy oxygen-rich water. Air stones and other aeration decor can be added.

Filtration: No special requirements, as long as the filter suits the size of the tank.

According to the study, Parotocinclus maculicauda is detritivorous. In the wild, its diet consists of a periphyton matrix (biofilm) – a complex community of microorganisms, algae and other organisms attached to submerged surfaces such as rocks, logs and plants.

In aquariums, the basis of the diet is popular dry foods (flakes, pellets). Plant-based foods and pieces of blanched vegetables (cucumber, lettuce leaves, zucchini, potatoes, broccoli, cabbage, carrots, etc.) should also be given regularly.

Good supplements are protein-rich live foods such as:

  • fresh or frozen brine shrimp (Artemia salina)
  • daphnia
  • grindal worms
  • cyclops, etc.

Although it can eat some algae (such as Green Dust Algae and Green Spot Algae), it is not as good at it as Otocinclus, so do not rely on it too much for algae control.

Feeding frequency: Adults should be fed once per day, with food that sinks to the bottom. The "five-minute rule" cannot be applied, as these fish eat slowly.

  • Diet type: omnivore (mostly herbivore)
  • Food preference: plant-based
  • Feeding frequency: daily

Temperament: Peaceful, calm, and not inclined to aggression or fin nipping.

Sociality: In nature they are usually found in large groups, so keeping a group is highly beneficial. Keep at least 6 or more individuals. In a group they behave more naturally and are less stressed; in small groups or alone they feel more vulnerable and are less active and social.

Activity: They are not shy, are very playful and fun to watch, especially when stirring up sediment clouds. They can be seen resting on large, flat rocks. As a diurnal species they prefer light during the day and rely heavily on vision to detect predators, food and conspecifics, but quickly retreat to darker areas when threatened.

Placement in tank: A bottom-dwelling species adapted to rocky streams, where they scavenge for food and hide in crevices and caves.

  • Social: yes
  • Activity: average
  • Placement: bottom-dwellers
  • Peaceful: yes
  • Nippers: no
  • Jumpers: no

Tankmates

A very friendly fish suitable for community tanks, as long as they have sufficient swimming space.

Fish: small or medium-sized fish with the same water requirements, such as neon tetras, Hemigrammus rhodostomus (brilliant rummynose tetra), pencilfish, harlequin rasboras, pygmy corydoras and Otocinclus.

Dwarf shrimp: They will not harm adult dwarf shrimp, but newly hatched shrimp may be eaten if caught. They are not persistent hunters and will not specifically chase shrimplets.

Snails: They can share a tank with any freshwater snail. If breeding them, snails may eat the eggs. Snails do not like soft, acidic water since it can erode their shells over time.

Avoid: large and/or aggressive and/or boisterous fish; all types of crayfish and most freshwater crabs.
Mature males have a visible genital papilla. In males, the tips of the pectoral fins reach the anal fin.

The reproductive process of this species is not even explored in scientific literature, and breeding in aquariums has proven difficult. According to the scarce information:

  • They reach sexual maturity at 6–8 months.
  • Parotocinclus maculicauda is an egg-scattering spawner.
  • Parents do not care for eggs and fry.
  • They need soft, acidic water for spawning.
  • Females usually release 5–10 translucent, yellow-green eggs and attach them to the undersides of plant leaves. The eggs are relatively large (about 2 mm) and more elliptical than those of Otocinclus.
  • Nutrients are absorbed quickly from the yolk sac, and fry hatch within 3–5 days.

Etymology: The genus name "Parotocinclus" combines the Greek "para" (near), "ous/otis" (ear) and "kinklis" (grid), referring to the perforated post-temporal bone. The species name "maculicauda" combines the Latin "macula" (spot) and "cauda" (tail).

Taxonomy: Family Loricariidae, order Siluriformes. The species was first described in 1877 by Franz Steindachner as Otocinclus maculicauda. In 1889 Parotocinclus was described by Eigenmann & Eigenmann as a monotypic subgenus of Hisonotus. In 1948 the species was renamed Parotocinclus steindachneri by Di Caporiacco, but the name was not accepted. In 1977, a genus revision found that Parotocinclus differs from Otocinclus by the presence of an adipose fin, and the species became Parotocinclus maculicauda.

Description: Adults reach about 4–6 cm total length in aquariums. Unlike Otocinclus, it possesses a tiny adipose fin. The head has no crests, depressions or tufts of denticles. It has 25–32 premaxillary teeth and 24–28 dentary teeth, and 23–25 lateral line plates. The abdomen is covered by three regular rows of large plates. The anal fin is truncate and the caudal fin strongly notched. A light brown lateral band runs from the snout to the caudal peduncle; the body above is light brown and below is yellowish with small black spots anteriorly. There are four transverse black bars (two beside the dorsal fin and two beside the adipose fin). The fin rays are light brown, regularly stained with black, with transparent membranes. A large irregular black blotch lies on the lower lobe of the caudal fin.

Lifespan: No data are available for the wild. In aquariums, with proper care, they live 4–5 years on average, depending on conditions, feeding and stress.

Rosado, and Lucy Seldin. “Cellulolytic potential of a novel strain of Paenibacillus sp. isolated from the armored catfish Parotocinclus maculicauda gut.” Brazilian Journal of Microbiology 42 (2011): 1608-1615.
  • Garavello, Julio. (1976). Systematics and geographical distribution of the genus Parotocinclus Eigenamnn & Eigenamnn, 1889 (Ostariophysi, Loricariidae). Arquivos de Zoologia. 28. 1. 10.11606/issn.2176-7793.v28i4p1-37.
  • Mazzoni, Rosana, Raquel Costa da Silva, and Míriam Plaza Pinto. “Invasion and colonisation of a tropical stream by an exotic loricariid fish: indices of gradual displacement of the native common pleco (Hypostomus punctatus) by the red fin dwarf pleco (Parotocinclus maculicauda) over fifteen years.” PloS one 10, no. 10 (2015): e0139968.
